subject: Medicine
stem: A 61-year-old man has 45 minutes of substernal pressure, sweating, and nausea. ECG shows new ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which myocardial territory is most directly implicated?

options.explanation: This lead pattern is not isolated right atrial injury.
These inferior leads view the diaphragmatic ventricular territory.
Anterior septal injury is chiefly reflected in early precordial leads.
High lateral changes are most directly seen in I and aVL.

explanation: Contiguous ST elevation in II, III, and aVF localizes an acute injury pattern to the inferior territory in this clinical context. The right coronary commonly supplies this region, but coronary anatomy varies and circumflex occlusion can also cause inferior infarction. ECG territory should not be equated with a guaranteed culprit artery.
objective: Localize inferior myocardial injury from contiguous inferior-lead ST elevation.
keyPoints: Localize inferior myocardial injury from contiguous inferior-lead ST elevation.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 76-year-old man has exertional syncope and chest discomfort. Examination shows a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids and a slow-rising pulse. Which valve lesion best fits?

options.explanation: Obstructed left ventricular outflow produces the characteristic radiation and pulse contour.
This usually produces a holosystolic apical murmur radiating toward the axilla.
This causes a diastolic rumble rather than this ejection murmur.
This is generally holosystolic and increases with inspiration.

explanation: Aortic stenosis produces a systolic ejection murmur as blood crosses an obstructed valve. Carotid radiation and a delayed low-amplitude upstroke support the diagnosis, while exertional symptoms indicate important hemodynamic limitation. Echocardiography is needed to quantify severity; auscultation alone cannot supply a reliable valve area.
objective: Recognize the combined murmur and pulse findings of aortic stenosis.
keyPoints: Recognize the combined murmur and pulse findings of aortic stenosis.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient with dyspnea has a blowing holosystolic murmur maximal at the apex and radiating to the left axilla. The murmur becomes louder with sustained handgrip. Which lesion is most likely?

options.explanation: This is an ejection murmur with characteristic carotid radiation.
This is best heard at the upper left sternal border and is an ejection murmur.
This produces a diastolic, not holosystolic, murmur.
Higher systemic resistance can increase systolic flow back into the left atrium.

explanation: Mitral regurgitation allows left ventricular blood to flow backward into the left atrium during systole, producing a holosystolic apical murmur. Handgrip increases afterload and can accentuate regurgitant flow. Murmur intensity is influenced by loading and lesion type, so imaging remains necessary to assess severity and cause.
objective: Identify mitral regurgitation from timing, location, radiation and handgrip response.
keyPoints: Identify mitral regurgitation from timing, location, radiation and handgrip response.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 28-year-old has sharp chest pain that worsens while supine and improves when leaning forward. A friction rub is heard, and ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. Which diagnosis best integrates the findings?

options.explanation: This does not typically produce positional pain with diffuse ST and PR changes.
A valve obstruction does not explain the acute inflammatory chest-pain syndrome.
Positional pleuritic pain, a rub and diffuse ECG changes support pericardial inflammation.
This usually gives a territorial rather than diffuse pattern and does not explain the rub as well.

explanation: Pericardial inflammation can cause sharp positional pain and a transient friction rub. Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression supports acute pericarditis, contrasting with a coronary-territory injury pattern. Evaluation must still consider myocardial involvement and hemodynamic complications; the ECG pattern alone does not establish an uncomplicated course.
objective: Integrate positional pain, friction rub and diffuse ECG changes in pericarditis.
keyPoints: Integrate positional pain, friction rub and diffuse ECG changes in pericarditis.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient with a large pericardial effusion becomes hypotensive with elevated jugular venous pressure. Systolic blood pressure falls 16 mm Hg during inspiration. Which mechanism best explains this exaggerated inspiratory fall?

options.explanation: Return varies with respiration but does not need to cease.

options.text: Constrained ventricular filling with increased ventricular interdependence
options.explanation: Inspiratory right-sided filling shifts the septum and reduces left ventricular filling.
Tamponade limits rather than permits free chamber expansion.

options.text: Sudden increase in left ventricular preload during inspiration
options.explanation: This is opposite to the fall in left-sided filling that reduces stroke volume.

explanation: In tamponade, elevated pericardial pressure limits total cardiac volume. Inspiration increases right-sided filling, shifting the septum and further limiting left ventricular filling and output. The resulting exaggerated inspiratory systolic pressure drop is pulsus paradoxus. Clinical and echocardiographic assessment determine whether an effusion is causing tamponade.
objective: Explain pulsus paradoxus through constrained filling and ventricular interaction.
keyPoints: Explain pulsus paradoxus through constrained filling and ventricular interaction.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A tall young adult develops sudden unilateral pleuritic pain and dyspnea. On the affected side, breath sounds are diminished and percussion is hyperresonant. He is hemodynamically stable. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.explanation: Pleural air reduces breath sounds and increases resonance.
Pleural fluid usually produces dullness rather than hyperresonance.
This often increases transmission of voice sounds and produces dullness.
This more often causes bilateral crackles than unilateral hyperresonance.

explanation: Air in the pleural space separates lung from chest wall, reducing transmitted breath sounds while producing hyperresonance. The abrupt unilateral presentation fits spontaneous pneumothorax. Hemodynamic stability does not prove the pneumothorax is trivial, and clinical deterioration would require prompt reassessment for tension physiology.
objective: Differentiate pleural air from pleural fluid using percussion and breath sounds.
keyPoints: Differentiate pleural air from pleural fluid using percussion and breath sounds.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient has progressive breathlessness. The right lung base is dull to percussion, breath sounds are reduced, and tactile fremitus is decreased. Which process best explains this examination pattern?

options.explanation: Air typically produces hyperresonance rather than marked dullness.

options.text: Open bronchus through consolidated lung alone
options.explanation: Consolidation commonly increases fremitus when the airway remains patent.
This does not usually create a localized dull area with reduced fremitus.

options.text: Pleural fluid separating lung from chest wall
options.explanation: Fluid dampens vibration transmission and produces percussion dullness.

explanation: Pleural fluid dampens transmitted vibrations and decreases breath sounds over the involved region. Dullness helps distinguish fluid from pleural air. Imaging confirms the collection, and fluid analysis may be required to determine its cause; examination alone cannot reliably classify a transudate versus an exudate.
objective: Recognize pleural effusion from dullness with reduced tactile fremitus.
keyPoints: Recognize pleural effusion from dullness with reduced tactile fremitus.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A woman develops sudden dyspnea after prolonged immobilization. Arterial blood gas shows hypoxemia and low PCO2 with an increased alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient. Which process best explains the hypoxemia if pulmonary embolism is confirmed?

options.text: Reduced inspired oxygen concentration at normal altitude
options.explanation: No change in inspired gas is described.

options.text: Complete absence of all alveolar ventilation
options.explanation: The low PCO2 indicates ongoing, often increased, overall ventilation.
Perfusion obstruction and redistributed flow impair effective matching across the lung.
This usually raises PCO2 and does not explain the elevated gradient by itself.

explanation: Pulmonary embolism produces heterogeneous ventilation-perfusion relationships through blocked and redistributed perfusion. Hyperventilation can lower PCO2 despite impaired oxygenation. The blood gas pattern is supportive but nonspecific; neither a low PCO2 nor an elevated A-a gradient confirms or excludes embolism without appropriate clinical assessment.
objective: Interpret hypoxemia with hypocapnia as compatible with V/Q mismatch, not pure hypoventilation.
keyPoints: Interpret hypoxemia with hypocapnia as compatible with V/Q mismatch, not pure hypoventilation.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A former smoker has chronic exertional dyspnea. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows persistently reduced FEV1/FVC and increased residual volume. Which physiologic pattern best explains the findings?

options.explanation: Anemia may cause dyspnea but does not directly lower FEV1/FVC.
Reduced expiratory flow and incomplete emptying increase residual volume.
Restriction requires reduced total lung capacity and usually preserves the ratio.
A persistently low expiratory ratio and air trapping indicate abnormal function.

explanation: Obstruction slows expiration, reducing FEV1 disproportionately to vital capacity and promoting air trapping. Increased residual volume supports incomplete emptying. A low forced vital capacity can occur from trapping and does not alone establish restriction; total lung capacity is needed when distinguishing obstruction from a mixed process.
objective: Interpret a low expiratory ratio with increased residual volume as obstructive physiology.
keyPoints: Interpret a low expiratory ratio with increased residual volume as obstructive physiology.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient with vomiting has orthostatic symptoms, dry mucosa, and rising creatinine. Before receiving fluids or diuretics, urine sodium is low and fractional sodium excretion is 0.4%. Which mechanism best explains the renal response?

options.text: Intact tubules avidly conserving sodium during reduced perfusion
options.explanation: Volume depletion activates sodium-retaining responses.

options.text: Complete loss of proximal and distal sodium transport
options.explanation: Severe transport failure would generally impair avid sodium conservation.
The stem does not describe a nephritic sediment.

options.text: Unregulated secretion of all filtered sodium
options.explanation: This contradicts the low measured urinary sodium excretion.

explanation: Reduced effective renal perfusion activates sympathetic and hormonal sodium retention when tubules remain functional. The clinical volume loss and low fractional sodium excretion support prerenal physiology. This measurement is not definitive in all settings; diuretics, chronic kidney disease, sepsis, and some intrinsic lesions can alter its interpretation.
objective: Interpret low fractional sodium excretion in a volume-depleted patient with intact tubular response.
keyPoints: Interpret low fractional sodium excretion in a volume-depleted patient with intact tubular response.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient with a lung malignancy has sodium 122 mEq/L, low serum osmolality, concentrated urine, and clinical euvolemia. Thyroid, adrenal, and renal function are adequate, and he takes no diuretic. Which mechanism best fits?

options.text: Absent ADH effect in the collecting duct
options.explanation: This would favor dilute high-volume urine and possible hypernatremia.
This does not explain the euvolemic hypotonic pattern with concentrated urine.
This would not directly generate hypotonic hyponatremia.

options.text: Persistent antidiuretic activity despite hypotonic plasma
options.explanation: Inappropriate water retention prevents normal urinary dilution.

explanation: SIADH is considered when hypotonic hyponatremia occurs with urine that remains inappropriately concentrated and an apparently euvolemic examination. Excluding adrenal, thyroid, renal, and medication causes is important. The mechanism is impaired free-water excretion, so low sodium concentration does not necessarily mean total-body sodium depletion.
objective: Recognize impaired free-water excretion in a compatible SIADH pattern.
keyPoints: Recognize impaired free-water excretion in a compatible SIADH pattern.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: After pituitary surgery, a patient develops high-volume dilute urine and rising serum sodium. Urine osmolality increases substantially after desmopressin. Which defect best explains the response?

options.explanation: This would generally favor water retention rather than dilute polyuria.
Osmotic diuresis usually contains substantial solute and is not defined by this hormone response.
Replacement hormone restores collecting-duct water permeability when the kidney can respond.
This would limit the response to administered desmopressin.

explanation: Central diabetes insipidus, also termed arginine vasopressin deficiency, produces inadequate antidiuretic signaling despite a responsive kidney. Desmopressin increases urine concentration, distinguishing this pattern from complete nephrogenic resistance. Postoperative fluid disorders can evolve over time, so serial sodium and volume assessment remain necessary.
objective: Use desmopressin responsiveness to localize impaired antidiuretic signaling.
keyPoints: Use desmopressin responsiveness to localize impaired antidiuretic signaling.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A young adult with diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain, glucose 420 mg/dL, high anion-gap acidosis, and elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate. Serum potassium is 5.3 mEq/L before therapy. Which statement about potassium is most accurate?

options.text: Potassium monitoring is unnecessary once insulin starts
options.explanation: Treatment can lower serum potassium and requires close monitoring.

options.text: Total-body potassium may be depleted despite the elevated serum value
options.explanation: Urinary losses coexist with shifts of potassium out of cells.

options.text: The high serum value proves large total-body potassium excess
options.explanation: Serum concentration does not directly quantify total-body stores.

options.text: Insulin will necessarily increase serum potassium further
options.explanation: Insulin generally promotes intracellular potassium movement.

explanation: In ketoacidosis, osmotic diuresis and vomiting can deplete potassium while insulin deficiency and extracellular shifts elevate its serum concentration. Insulin treatment and correction of the metabolic disturbance can reveal substantial hypokalemia. The initial serum level therefore must not be mistaken for a measurement of total-body potassium sufficiency.
objective: Distinguish serum potassium from total-body stores in diabetic ketoacidosis.
keyPoints: Distinguish serum potassium from total-body stores in diabetic ketoacidosis.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient has resistant hypertension, spontaneous hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Testing shows high aldosterone with suppressed renin under appropriate sampling conditions. Which mechanism explains the low renin?

options.text: Autonomous aldosterone causes sodium retention and volume expansion
options.explanation: Expanded effective circulating volume suppresses renin release.
That would tend to raise renin and suggests a secondary aldosterone process.
This would not explain high aldosterone with hypertension and potassium loss.

options.text: Loss of all distal sodium transport
options.explanation: This would oppose mineralocorticoid-driven sodium retention.

explanation: Primary aldosterone excess increases distal sodium reabsorption and promotes potassium and hydrogen ion loss. Resulting volume expansion suppresses renin, distinguishing primary from many secondary causes. Medication effects, potassium status, and sampling conditions can influence testing, so a screening ratio requires appropriate clinical interpretation.
objective: Distinguish autonomous aldosterone excess by suppressed renin and potassium wasting.
keyPoints: Distinguish autonomous aldosterone excess by suppressed renin and potassium wasting.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient has vomiting of blood followed by black, tarry stools. He has not taken iron or bismuth. Which interpretation best fits the stool appearance in this clinical context?

options.explanation: Hemorrhoids more often cause bright red bleeding and do not explain hematemesis.

options.text: Proof that bleeding has completely stopped
options.explanation: Stool color alone cannot establish cessation or hemodynamic stability.

options.text: A normal stool variant requiring no assessment
options.explanation: Concurrent hematemesis indicates clinically important gastrointestinal bleeding.
Upper tract bleeding commonly produces black tarry stool after blood digestion.

explanation: Melena reflects altered blood in the gastrointestinal tract and commonly accompanies upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Hematemesis strongly supports an upper source here. Melena is not perfectly source-specific and can persist after bleeding slows, so clinical assessment and appropriate investigation remain necessary rather than judging activity from color alone.
objective: Interpret melena with hematemesis while recognizing limits of stool appearance.
keyPoints: Interpret melena with hematemesis while recognizing limits of stool appearance.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient develops jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and pruritus. Alkaline phosphatase is disproportionately elevated compared with aminotransferases. Which biochemical process best explains the dark urine?

options.explanation: This would not explain jaundice with bilirubinuria.

options.text: Increased urinary intact erythrocytes as the sole cause
options.explanation: Hematuria would not explain the full cholestatic pattern.

options.text: Urinary excretion of water-soluble conjugated bilirubin
options.explanation: Conjugated bilirubin can enter plasma and be filtered during cholestasis.
Unconjugated bilirubin is not ordinarily filtered in urine.

explanation: Cholestasis can raise circulating conjugated bilirubin, which is water soluble and can be excreted in urine. Reduced delivery of bile pigments to the gut contributes to pale stools. The laboratory pattern suggests cholestasis but does not alone distinguish an extrahepatic obstruction from every intrahepatic cholestatic cause.
objective: Explain bilirubinuria through conjugated, rather than unconjugated, bilirubin.
keyPoints: Explain bilirubinuria through conjugated, rather than unconjugated, bilirubin.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a serum lipase four times the upper reference limit. Which combination is sufficient to meet the usual diagnostic framework for acute pancreatitis without requiring imaging in every case?

options.text: Mandatory abnormal CT before recognizing any case
options.explanation: Imaging is useful selectively but is not required when other criteria are met.

options.text: Typical pain plus pancreatic enzyme elevation above three times the upper limit
options.explanation: Two compatible criteria can establish the diagnosis in an appropriate setting.

options.text: Any abdominal discomfort plus a minimally increased lipase
options.explanation: Mild elevations are nonspecific and do not meet the stated enzyme threshold.
A normal result by itself does not establish pancreatitis.

explanation: Acute pancreatitis is commonly diagnosed when at least two of three features are present: characteristic pain, substantial pancreatic enzyme elevation, or compatible imaging. This vignette supplies the first two. Imaging may still be needed for uncertainty or complications, and enzyme magnitude does not reliably measure disease severity.
objective: Apply the two-of-three diagnostic framework without equating enzyme magnitude with severity.
keyPoints: Apply the two-of-three diagnostic framework without equating enzyme magnitude with severity.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient with cirrhosis develops confusion and asterixis after several days of constipation. No focal neurologic deficit is found. Which mechanism is most consistent with hepatic encephalopathy?

options.text: Impaired hepatic handling of gut-derived neuroactive substances
options.explanation: Portosystemic shunting and reduced detoxification contribute to brain dysfunction.

options.text: Asterixis proves a single measured ammonia value is diagnostic
options.explanation: Asterixis and ammonia values are not uniquely diagnostic.

options.text: Direct compression of the brain by ascites
options.explanation: Ascites does not mechanically compress the brain.

options.text: Complete elimination of gut bacterial metabolism
options.explanation: Constipation does not eliminate production of gut-derived nitrogen compounds.

explanation: Hepatic dysfunction and portosystemic shunting permit gut-derived substances to contribute to altered brain function. Constipation can be a precipitant, but infection, bleeding, medications, and other causes of confusion must also be considered. Ammonia is involved mechanistically, yet a blood concentration alone does not diagnose or grade the syndrome reliably.
objective: Understand hepatic encephalopathy while avoiding ammonia-only diagnosis.
keyPoints: Understand hepatic encephalopathy while avoiding ammonia-only diagnosis.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: An older adult has persistent back pain, anemia, hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, and multiple lytic bone lesions. Serum studies show a monoclonal protein. Which diagnosis best integrates the findings?

options.explanation: This does not explain monoclonal protein, lytic lesions and hypercalcemia.
This affects coagulation rather than producing this multisystem pattern.
A platelet proliferative disorder does not best explain this combination.
Clonal plasma-cell disease can cause lytic bone injury and end-organ damage.

explanation: Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell disorder associated with monoclonal protein and characteristic organ injury, including anemia, bone lesions, hypercalcemia, and kidney dysfunction. A monoclonal protein alone can occur without symptomatic myeloma, so the associated findings and formal marrow and diagnostic evaluation matter.
objective: Recognize monoclonal plasma-cell disease with attributable end-organ injury.
keyPoints: Recognize monoclonal plasma-cell disease with attributable end-organ injury.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient with severe sepsis develops oozing from intravenous sites. Platelets are low, PT and aPTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is reduced, and D-dimer is elevated. Which mechanism best explains the combined bleeding and thrombosis risk?

options.explanation: DIC involves excessive systemic activation rather than complete absence of clotting.

options.text: Pure platelet receptor blockade without factor consumption
options.explanation: This does not explain prolonged coagulation tests and low fibrinogen.

options.text: Systemic coagulation activation with consumption of platelets and factors
options.explanation: Microvascular clotting and factor depletion can occur together.

options.text: Isolated lack of factor VIII only
options.explanation: This would not typically lower platelets and fibrinogen with this broad pattern.

explanation: DIC involves widespread coagulation activation, fibrin formation, and secondary fibrinolysis. Consumption of platelets and coagulation factors can produce bleeding even while microthrombi threaten organ perfusion. The laboratory pattern is interpreted with the underlying illness and trends; no single result captures every stage of DIC.
objective: Explain simultaneous microthrombosis and consumptive bleeding in DIC.
keyPoints: Explain simultaneous microthrombosis and consumptive bleeding in DIC.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient suddenly develops right facial and arm weakness with expressive language impairment. Leg strength is relatively preserved. In a person with typical left-hemisphere language dominance, which arterial territory is most consistent?

options.explanation: This would more often suggest brainstem or broader posterior circulation findings.
Lateral motor cortex and dominant language regions fit this distribution.
This more often affects the left leg and does not explain dominant expressive aphasia.
This mainly threatens occipital visual regions rather than the described motor-language pattern.

explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies much of the lateral cerebral hemisphere, including face-arm motor areas and dominant language cortex. Sudden contralateral face-arm weakness with aphasia therefore suggests a left MCA event. Emergency imaging is required to distinguish ischemia from hemorrhage and guide treatment; localization alone does not establish the pathology.
objective: Localize face-arm weakness with aphasia to the dominant MCA territory.
keyPoints: Localize face-arm weakness with aphasia to the dominant MCA territory.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A woman has fluctuating ptosis and diplopia that worsen late in the day. Sensation and tendon reflexes are preserved. Antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors are detected. Which site is primarily affected?

options.explanation: Reduced functional receptor availability impairs transmission during repeated use.

options.text: Dorsal columns of the spinal cord
options.explanation: This would affect vibration and position sensation rather than isolated fatigable weakness.
This mechanism causes disinhibition rather than typical receptor-antibody fatigability.
This would more often cause spasticity and pathologic reflexes.

explanation: Myasthenia gravis commonly involves antibody-mediated loss or dysfunction of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, reducing the safety margin of neuromuscular transmission. Ocular and bulbar symptoms can fluctuate with use, while sensation remains intact. Preserved reflexes and the antibody finding help distinguish it from several central and presynaptic disorders.
objective: Localize fatigable weakness with receptor antibodies to the postsynaptic junction.
keyPoints: Localize fatigable weakness with receptor antibodies to the postsynaptic junction.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient with severe infection remains hypotensive after appropriate initial volume assessment and has warm extremities early in the course. Which hemodynamic abnormality most directly characterizes the distributive component of septic shock?

options.text: Fixed severe elevation of systemic resistance in every phase
options.explanation: This is not the defining distributive abnormality.

options.text: Mechanical obstruction of all pulmonary outflow
options.explanation: This describes obstructive rather than distributive shock.

options.text: Primary absence of circulating blood volume as the only mechanism
options.explanation: Sepsis includes vascular and cellular abnormalities beyond simple fluid loss.
Inflammatory vasodilation lowers vascular tone despite variable cardiac output.

explanation: Septic shock often includes inflammatory vasodilation with reduced systemic vascular resistance, altered microcirculation, and capillary leak. Cardiac output may be high or low depending on phase and myocardial function. Warm skin is compatible with early distributive physiology but does not by itself diagnose sepsis or exclude severe perfusion impairment.
objective: Identify reduced vascular resistance as the distributive component of septic shock.
keyPoints: Identify reduced vascular resistance as the distributive component of septic shock.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient has hemoptysis, hypoxemia, rapidly rising creatinine, and red-cell casts. Kidney immunofluorescence shows smooth linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. Which mechanism best fits?

options.explanation: This does not explain pulmonary hemorrhage with glomerular casts.
This would not produce linear IgG deposition and nephritic sediment.

options.text: Antibodies directed against basement membrane antigens
options.explanation: Shared target structures can produce alveolar and glomerular injury.

options.text: Granular deposited circulating immune complexes only
options.explanation: The linear pattern supports direct binding rather than a typical granular complex pattern.

explanation: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease can injure both renal and pulmonary capillary basement membranes, producing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and alveolar hemorrhage. Smooth linear immunofluorescence reflects antibody binding along the target structure. Not every pulmonary-renal syndrome is anti-GBM disease; other vasculitic and immune-complex processes require distinction.
objective: Connect a pulmonary-renal syndrome and linear IgG to anti-GBM injury.
keyPoints: Connect a pulmonary-renal syndrome and linear IgG to anti-GBM injury.
attribution: OpenPrep contributors; AI-assisted original educational content (2026). No clinician review claimed.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient develops an acutely painful, swollen knee with fever and severe pain on passive movement. Synovial fluid is cloudy with many neutrophils. Which conclusion is most appropriate while cultures are pending?

options.text: Severe passive-motion pain proves a chronic tendon disorder
options.explanation: This pattern raises concern for an intra-articular acute process.

options.text: Joint infection requires urgent evaluation even if crystals are also found
options.explanation: Crystal arthritis and infection can coexist, and cartilage injury can progress rapidly.

options.text: The presence of any crystals completely excludes infection
options.explanation: Crystals do not rule out concomitant septic arthritis.

options.text: A normal radiograph excludes early infection
options.explanation: Early septic arthritis may have no diagnostic plain-film changes.

explanation: An acutely inflamed joint with fever and painful passive motion warrants prompt evaluation for septic arthritis. Synovial testing, including culture, is central, and neither crystals nor an initially normal radiograph safely excludes infection. Neutrophil counts support the assessment but overlap between infectious and noninfectious causes prevents a single-count diagnosis.
objective: Avoid excluding septic arthritis solely because crystals or normal early radiographs are present.
keyPoints: Avoid excluding septic arthritis solely because crystals or normal early radiographs are present.
